metadata.title: Tables That Say Only What the Chapter Says
metadata.note: Week 6 how-to video. Voice hai/Bella for @HumanitariansAI. Content only from the table-building chat; no claim about when any table was built.
metadata.author: Risa Samanta

beats.narration_text: A table in a textbook is not just a grid. It has to match the house style, say only what the chapter says, and come with a preview someone can check. This is Risa Samanta's how-to video for the week: turning a table from a report into a finished table file.

props.command: claude "build the chapter 25 tables like my chapter 14 table file, and give me a PDF preview"
output: one finished table as the style template

beats.narration_text: The recipe is simple. Give Claude one finished table file as the style template, plus the audit report whose entries are marked type table. For chapter twenty-five that produced two table files, the TKI target classification and the biomarker type classification, plus a PDF preview of both.

props.title: inputs and outputs
props.code:
inputs
  ch14_visual11.mdx        finished table: the style template
  its preview image
  CAJAL_Chapter25.docx     the audit: entries marked Type: Table

outputs
  ch25_visual6.mdx         TKI Target Classification
  ch25_visual18.mdx        Biomarker Type Classification
  ch25_tables_preview.pdf  preview of both
props.sparkLine: One finished table teaches the style.

beats.narration_text: The file itself is plain MDX: a styled container, an italic caption, then the table. It uses the same fonts, shading and callout colors as the chapter fourteen template, so every table in the book looks like it belongs.

props.title: ch25_visual6.mdx, first lines
props.code: Table 1. Major classes of tyrosine kinase inhibitors by molecular target. ...

beats.narration_text: The style carries meaning. In the chapter fourteen table, red marks the one row where the source text names a negative finding, and blue marks a working mechanism. The chapter twenty-five tables have no red at all, because the chapter names nothing negative in them. That was a question worth asking, not a bug.

props.command: claude "why is there no red in the chapter 25 tables?"

beats.narration_text: The rule that matters most is to say only what the chapter says. In chapter twenty-three, the chemotherapy table has no G1 row, because the chapter mentions G1 only as checkpoint biology and names no G1-specific drug class. In chapter thirty-two, two glioblastoma subtypes get a gray note instead of a treatment response, because the source gives none. A missing row is a decision someone can see and reverse.
beats.visual_intent: Real drifted caption names from the actual repo animating toward a clean sectioned scheme. Show the mechanism, not a count.

lines.text: no G1 row: the chapter names no G1-specific drug class
treatment response for two GBM subtypes (Chapter 32)
gray italic note: the source gives none

beats.narration_text: Every table also comes with a PDF preview, so a reviewer can read it before it goes into the chapter. And each one gets a placement instruction: which file, and after which line. Table twenty-three point five point two goes at the end of the tumor microenvironment subsection, between line one twenty-six and the next heading.

props.command: claude "where does Table 23.5.2 go in the 23.5 file?"

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Give Claude one finished table as the template, and the list of tables to build. Ask it to build only what the source text supports, to list anything it left out, and to give you a preview. Then check the left-out list first.

props.command: claude "here is a finished table as the template. build the tables on this list from the source text only, and list anything you left out"

beats.narration_text: Tables that say only what the chapter says. This has been Risa Samanta's how-to, voiced by Bella for Humanitarians AI. Check the left-out list first.
